I’m not familiar with ones done on COPD and secondary smoke, but if you find some and read them, don’t forget to consider the funding background and motivations of the researchers involved. Question: How is second-hand smoking defined when it comes to cigars or cigarettes?
Answer: First off, recognize that it’s basically a “made-up” term designed for a specific political and emotional effect. “second-hand” (or “secondhand”) implies something that was used and then cast off (usually as dirty or unwanted) by a primary user. “Secondhand smoking” is basically what occurs if you are in the same air-space as a present or past active smoker. Any submicroscopic trace of the combustion products of tobacco smoke in the air where someone is or has been smoking would be defined as second-hand smoke if a nonsmoker entered the air space and inhaled it… technically and rather loosely even if the tobacco were being burned as “incense” for those who enjoy its scent. Secondhand smoking is a term rarely applied to anything other than tobacco (occasionally, but rarely, marijuana) and is applied, prejudicially, even if the level of exposure is on the order of one-one-thousandth of a typical smoker’s total exposure. Heh, I brought a little gathering of folks to a club in Philadelphia at one point just as it was opening after being closed for over 12 hours — only to have someone leave because the “secondhand smoke” was making it difficult for them to breathe — despite there having been no lit tobacco there for over 12 hours and had had it’s air exchanged dozens of times in the gap! So, it’s smoke that is used, cast off as unwanted, and more or less “identical” to smoke being blown directly in one’s face or inhaled directly by a smoker from a lit product. It’s generally not a term that was historically applied to anything else until it was ramped up for organized propagana. Think I’m exaggerating? Take a look at this N-Gram: Google Books Ngram Viewer to see how it was used in the creation of and push for smoking bans in the 1970s after a Sir George Godber hosted one of the first large international antismoking conferences in 1973: Before then it only existed as more or less a “joke term”. See my freely printable booklet, The Lies Behind The Smoking Bans, at and feel free to print and share it if you like. Question: Can smoking one cigarette per day lead to lung cancer? How long does it take for lung damage to occur after quitting smoking?
Answer: (NOTE: I am not a doctor, nor do I have any medical training. I have however done thousands of hours of research on the general topic of cigarette smoking and the risks of such things as “secondhand” and “thirdhand” smoke, and written two books on the topic.) The answer could be yes if you accept the idea that sticking your hand out the front door once a day in the morning where a carcinogenic sunbeam might hit it could lead to skin cancer: There Is NO SAFE LEVEL of exposure to sunshine! (At least in terms of skin cancer.) The average nonsmoker would have a lifetime average of between about a 0.1% to perhaps a 1% chance of getting lung cancer just by ordinary breathing of air ranging from countryside to modern cities. The average pack-a-day smoker who smokes for 50 years (say, from age 15 to 65), would, depending on all sorts of other factors, generally stand a 5% to 20% chance of getting lung cancer, with most of them closer to the 5% than 20%. But, taking the 20% as our general worst case figure, that’s 365 x 50 x 20, or 365,000 cigarettes producing a 20% lifetime chance. Your smoking of 1 a day would increase your (roughly) 0.5% chance to about 1 or 1.5%. NOTE: figures at the extremes in this sort of statistics question tend to be VERY inaccurate (or even just silly) because of a number of different factors, but with smoking it seems to have very little effect at very low levels or short times when compared to the very high levels for multiple decades. And exposures to such active carcinogens as asbestos fibers can play a very big role themselves. I would not be surprised to find a 50% figure for lifetime heavy-smoking asbestos workers! NOTE ALSO: Very few people ever go through life smoking one cigarette per day. Low levels of smoking tend to be very enjoyable, producing sort of a temporary “high” that lasts for up to several minutes. Because it feels good, most people want to repeat it and end up smoking more… usually up in the range of ten to thirty a day. And at ten to thirty a day for multiple decades the risk becomes something most people would reasonably feel concerned about. In terms of secondary smoke exposure, it is MUCH lower than Antismokers generally rant ’n rave about. See the archived version of my page for Dissecting Antismokers’ Brains at Dissecting Antismokers' Brains and, in particular, the page on secondary smoke at ETS Exposure .I think you’ll agree, considering the risks noted above for smoking one cigarette per day compared to 20, that any normal exposures to ETS in decently ventilated conditions is low enough for normal folks not to actively “worry” about it in making their life decisions. For secondary smoke concerns, think about this: If you had two job offers, offers that were roughly equal except Job (B) paid a little bit more than Job (A), what value/concern/worry would you attach to the fact that getting to Job (B) each day required you to cross 11 streets, while Job (A) <with longer blocks> only required 10 such crossings. Would you worry about the extra chance of horrible mangled death you’d face each day from crossing that one extra street to get to Job (B)? It’s a clear and inarguable difference of threat… but it’s at a level that most of us would consider mental illness to actively worry about when compared to other variables concerning the decision!

Question: What should I do when my current boyfriend says he is not into me sexually and romantically anymore and just wants me to be friends? We've been great together and I didn't any precious sign and I still love him so much and can't move on?
Answer: Assuming he’s being honest and knows his own feelings, you need to first of all realize he’s NOT in any sense trying to hurt you: he’s probably hurting an awful lot in being honest with you rather than simply disappearing or trying to invent a big fight or etc etc. While part of what you’ll feel will certainly be anger and confusion, you will really do what’s best for the two of you if you can keep the anger controlled: remember, he’s not doing this because he wants to hurt you or because he’s decided he hates you or anything at all like that: He’s simply realized that he’s changed over the years or that your relationship with him has changed and that it’ll be best for the two of you if you can acknowledge and accept that change even though you still care for him just as you always have. Let him know that while you’re not going to scream and fight with him because of it, that hearing this from him HAS hurt you and (at this point at least) your life a lot and it’ll probably be a lot easier for both of you if you, at least for a rough time period, agree to try to make it easy to avoid each other in social situations until things change or at least until your feelings have receded to the point where you can share a space without having your thoughts and emotions regarding him overwhelming anything else you could do socially. While it may feel hard to believe right now, it IS possible that despite everything you may currently feel that he will play a part in your future life as a close friend. And if you handle that guide well… you may, unexpectedly for either or both of you… end up together and happy again! Unlikely? Maybe. But only the future knows.

Question: What is the worst pain you ever felt in your lifetime?
Answer: The worst pain, paradoxically, was also fairly unimportant or even that upsetting once I discovered what it was. It came from what’s sometimes called an “Icepick Headache” — i.e. a pain in the head area that most often is intermittent, sometimes (often?) caused by allergies, **VERY** scary… but also **VERY BRIEF**! It is SO brief that it’s almost hard to think of it AS pain although it very clearly IS, and is right at the top of the charts in my own experience. In my case, several times a year, sometimes though with a full year or more between, I would suddenly get exactly the sort of pain you’d expect if you were tied up and someone stabbed you deeply in the eye with an icepick. Thus the name of the “headache.” I began experiencing it in my 20s and did not discover its cause and cure until my mid 30s when I noticed a peculiar cluster that seemed to occur only in periods when I was hanging out with a certain group of friends. I tried to think of how that could possibly be the cause… and the only thing that stood out as different was that these friends loved to sit around and chat over bottles of white wine!!! I was allergic to white wine! Although to this day I have no idea what type even just a single additional experience of that flash of pain more than overcomes any desire I might have for pinpointing the variety! I think others who’ve experienced icepick headaches may agree with me on the pain intensity, although, strangely, they’re also “not that bad” in a way. Why do I say that? Simple: the pain was SOOOO fast/instantaneous/passing that it was *almost* as though it wasn’t real. It was simply unthinkable (although still horrifically scary) to consider what pain at that level lasting even a full second in time would have been like: literally a pain that would drive someone to a quick suicide just to stop it. The duration is so brief that it is almost as though you have SEEN the pain… as of a flash of a camera lightbulb… rather than experienced the feeling of it.

Question: What happens when people who don't smoke crack secondhand inhale it?
Answer: Since, just like with tobacco smoke, the contact with secondary smoke will be on the order of 1/100th down to 1/100,000th or so of the amount of smoke the actual smoker will inhale and absorb while trying to hold it in… … “the happens” thing will be virtually nonexistent other than the incredibly small amounts of odoriferous substances that our noses are able to detect down to something like one one-millionth of a part of air. I’m not a doctor and smoke nothing but tobacco, but that’s about how it will work out. You simply don’t get measurable effects worth normal human lifetime consideration from such exposures. Even the most extreme tobacco smoke exposures — a lifetime of workplace daily exposures for 8 hours a day, 5 days a week, for a working lifetime in the 1940s through 1990s period “when EVERYONE smoked” (Heh, not *really* everyone… but it sure seemed that way!) even with THAT level of exposure, the best the EPA was able to claim in its big Report years ago was that out of 1,000 people exposed to 80,000 hours of such strong exposure over forty years there would be no more than ONE extra case of lung cancer (LC was used for the study since it was seen as by far the most sensitive and unique barometer of whatever effect might have existed.) Heh, unfortunately for the EPA, even that 1 after 80,000 hours of exposure couldn’t pass the minimum test for statistical significance, so in normal science it would have been just ignored. Of course with tobacco smoke then or crack smoke now, you’re not dealing with “normal science” in these sorts of analyses. You’ll likely find things claiming that there are worrisome effects, and those conclusions will have been reached by ignoring basic scientific approaches to analysis or the simple deceptive misuse of language in describing research results in ways designed to terrify the average layperson.

If you drive a gas-powered car or live in an area polluted by drivers or such, if you’re around people who intentionally smoke just about anything, and probably if you blow out your birthday candles each year and inhale traces of smoke from those blown-out candles… or all of those combined could, in some sense of meaning, be said to have contributed as a “cause” for a person getting emphysema. The amount of smoking you describe would likely have no or almost no measurable effect in pretty much all the non-AAT-1 population (i.e. better than 99% of the population) although with any such medical statistical things it might still get listed as a “contributing factor” or somesuch. NOTE: I am NOT a doctor, nor do I have medical training of any kind, although I’ve read and written extensively about the effects of smoking and exposure to other folks’ smoke. Question: My friends are huge cigarette smokers. I’ve never smoked in my life, but I plan to. Will being exposed to so much smoke (as 75% of my friends smoke) affect my lungs as well in the long term?

That study found an increase of 1 case of lung cancer for every thousand workers exposed to constant daily workplace smoke for 80,000 hours back before worries about ventilation for such was a big thing. Even to come up with THAT extraordinarily weak “threat” as an actual finding, the researchers had to juggle normal scientific standards because the study failed at the usual “95% correlation” standard that usually serves as a base for further research. So your exposure as a young person hanging with friends who are “huge” smokers is highly, *HIGHLY* unlikely to have a carcinogenic effect upon your lungs in general. In terms of other health hazards, they were not generally found at even this small level, although about one person in every 2,500 has a genetic defect called Alpha-Antitrypsin Deficiency (AAT-1), and will likely suffer from a significant level of COPD as they age and are exposed to any sort of air pollution from cooking, smoking, or urban living. Whether it’s worth worrying about such things is up to each of us as we go through life. If you have a choice between two jobs, with one being a block closer to where you live, taking the closer job likely reduces your lifetime risk of being torn limb from limb and thrown into the gutter from crossing that extra street twice a day for forty years. Should you worry about that and take the concern as significant enough to turn down a “better” job? That should be up to you, and only you, in making such a decision — although I’ll confess to having been a fairly strong anti-driving bicyclist over the years who, in the past, would like to have taken that freedom from you.

Question: How does smoking cessation and avoiding exposure to secondhand smoke significantly improve lung health?
Answer: Long answer here, with references, so before diving in, let me note that unlike some in the antismoking community, I am upfront about NOT being a medical doctor or practitioner of any type, matter, or form at all, OK? Now, to the Question itself: Primary smoking adds stress to the heart and lungs, most particularly when done regularly and in quantity. Stopping smoking should indeed significantly improve the health of one’s lungs over one’s lifetime. However, the usual exposure to secondary smoke has virtually no inherent effect on lung health at levels one would normally be exposed to today in Free Choice situations, though the classic super-smoky bar or poker game, particularly if engaged in very regularly might have some small effect, and effects in a small proportion of lung-compromised people can be notable. It should also be noted though that the smoke from the end of a burning cigarette, if held up to one’s nose and inhaled directly in concentration, is significantly “worse” than that which is produced at a higher puff temperature and filtered through a cigarette and/or filter, However, that smoke is heavily diluted, usually by a factor of 100 to 100,000 times by the type and circumstances of the exposure. You can read more about that online at my book site at Dissecting Antismokers' Brains The two exceptions to the above regarding secondary smoke occur with regard to lung cancer incidence where the classic EPA Report of the 1990s that resulted in so many of the original smoking bans claimed a normally non-significant statistical relationship between a lifetime of heavy work exposure (Think in terms of 1940s through 1980s work situations where smoking bans were virtually unknown outside of dynamite factories and oxygen wards in hospitals!) and lung cancer, where such a lifetime showed a possible increase in occurrence about 4 in 1,000 to about 5 in 1,000 nonsmokers … i.e. an increase of one in a thousand after 80,000 hours of intense exposure. See the original Report at Note that usually, for public consumption for desired effect, the usual message is simply expressed as “Exposure to secondhand smoke increases your risk to lung cancer by 19%” — leading most folks to end up thinking that passing by someone smoking in a park gives them a 20% chance of death! LOL! Language and phrasing is a powerful tool, particularly when combined with fear, in reaching into and “adjusting” someone’s mind — and we’ve seen the results all too clearly in the common reactions today to secondary smoke exposure. Other than that one very questionably “significant” finding, the EPA came up with nothing, and an international study by the World Health Organization meant to improve their findings instead accomplished the opposite! See Multicenter case-control study of exposure to environmental tobacco smoke and lung cancer in Europe - PubMed for the WHO study covering seven European countries that *DID* find a significant finding: I.E. a .78 ratio between exposures and lung cancer: I.E. exposed individuals got 22% LESS lung cancer than non-exposed individuals. Given the highly publicized nature of the study by a body as prestigious as the WHO, the findings couldn’t simply be covered up… … but note the phrasing in the Abstract: “ETS exposure during childhood was not associated with an increased risk of lung cancer (odds ratio [OR] for ever exposure = 0.78; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.64-0.96).“ The ONE significant finding in the study, if it had been applied to almost anything else, would have been taken as a significant sign of early exposure conferring some sort of immunity to long term harms! But of course that’s NOT the message that the World Health Organization wanted to put out in public, particularly not if its researchers ever wanted to see another single solitary cent in antismoking funding! Heh, the EPA Report was not able to come up with a significant finding in the opposite direction, yet the entire wave of publicity about it made it sound like it had made such a finding and eventually resulted in those 1990s’ smoking bans! Soooo… at least in terms of lung cancer, which is generally accepted as about the deadliest disease from smoking and the disease most particularly and directly related to smoking statistically as well, “smoking cessation” can have a direct effect, but for the average person in normal smoke-exposed circumstances, the cessation of such exposure seems unlikely to generally related to usually perceptible levels of “lung health.” Note that the above paragraph doesn’t mean that delicate laboratory tests and measurements can’t find a difference, nor does it mean that decades upon decades of heavy exposure would have no effect at all… but what it DOES mean is that in most circumstances for most people such exposures are likely to be meaningless in the course of their daily life. Your risk of getting a deadly hit by by a car while crossing a street is likely far, far greater! P.S. Question: What are the symptoms of nicotine addiction? How long does it take for the body to get used to the nicotine after starting to smoke cigarettes? I'm 17 and on my 2nd pack and no longer cough, but I feel normal without cravings. Will I get hooked?
Answer: Mats Andersson’s answer is, as is usual with Mats, thoughtful and insightful. However, in this instance I would largely disagree with him. His characterization of nicotine may well be true for some people, but I believe it differs strongly from one person to another. My father smoked between one and two packs a day for about 55 years. But he gave it up every year for Lent. Mats, have you ever known a heroin addict or crack addict who gave up their vice every year for a few weeks as a religious gesture and then happily returned to it? And while I was aware he was doing this each year, I never noticed that he was going through any sort of hardship or disturbance or pangs during the weeks of Lent. I drank a fairly large amount of beer from my late teens through my 30s, and a large amount of vodka from my 30s through my 60s. But I was a social drinker: I drank to be with my friends at the local pubs. The smoking ban knocked out several of my favorite pubs — not because I couldn’t smoke but because I couldn’t stand to see so many people interrupting their evenings to go stand outside to smoke. Seeing what the Antismokers had accomplished, a degree of control over people’s normal behaviors and lives, simply by dint of hundreds of millions of dollars of government antismoking funding was disturbing… deeply disturbing… and it was a feeling that was reinforced every single time I saw someone get up from their group to go stand outside no matter the weather … well, seeing that over and over and over again was just too miserable — particularly because everyone cooperated so easily with what Big Brother Government was suddenly dictating. That discomfort limited me to just a few pubs in my area and COVID limited that even more… so I ended up basically kicking my pub habit and simply staying at home for a good part of the last few years. Did I miss my social contacts? Very much so. Did I go into withdrawals from drinking? Not at all: I obviously could have just drunk vodka at home. But I had no incentive to: I drank to be social with others who were drinking, and drinking at home didn’t contribute to that. I’d say I probably drank two to three bottles of wine per year since early 2020 as opposed to two to three per month before then. So alcohol, with a potential for addiction that is so strong that hospitals know to watch out for withdrawals leading into life-threatening spasms, despite the strength of its addictive hold on a seemingly large subset of the population, presented me with no problem at all concerning withdrawals. Mats, where we differ is my staunch belief that “addiction” is largely individualized rather than rule of thumb chemical, when it comes to most people. Your advice may be quite sound for some, maybe even many, people out there. But for some others, maybe even many others, I believe it greatly overstates the amount of dependence that we classically associate with true addiction.

Question: I have parents who smoke. How can I reduce breathing in secondhand smoke?
Answer: Very simple if you’re old enough to spend your relaxed time outside the house. Just go out. If you’re not old enough and you have your own room and aren’t forced to share a bedroom/study-room etc with them all day and night, then pick up one of those small fans (5″ types, cheap on Amazon) and put it in a window in your room (set with side cushions or panels easily made from cardboard boxes if you have nothing else) and have it blow fresh air into the room. You don’t need very much at all to create a positive air pressure that will keep the smoke out: smoke is NOT “magical” (no matter what you hear from some of the crazies out there) and it will not grow little smoky arms and legs and swim its way upstream and under the crack at the bottom of your door simply to attack you. Those approaches in and of themselves should reduce what you’re “breathing in” by a very good amount. Now… there’s a question hanging in the eaves: You use the term “breathing in” rather than terms like “dealing with the smell.” That makes it sound like you are worried about “breathing in” the smoke. Unless you have a genetic defect known as AAT-1 that predisposes you toward COPD or unless you’re in a poorly heated/cooled tightly enclosed small living space all day and night with your parents or have some other unusual diagnosed lung/breathing condition you don’t really have much of anything to be concerned about health/life wise, particularly not when you consider what else you’re facing on a daily basis in your life. And actually, if you believe in the integrity and authority of the United Nations and the World Health Organization, the massive international study they did on secondary smoke exposure with Dr. Boffetta back in 1998 looked at “passive exposure to smoke” (what the Nazis called “Passivrauchen” in their short-lived antismoking campaign), the WHO found NO significant health effects of exposure from spouses or workplaces or living or social situations with ONE very significant exception: They found that children of smokers ended up later in life with 22% LESS lung cancer than children of nonsmokers. Ever hear of the Bubble Boy Syndrome? It’s believed that children who are raised in environments that are “too clean” end up with bodily defensive systems later in life that seem to be underdeveloped… leaving those poor children defenseless against the biological challenges they’ll have to face in later life. Healthwise, on balance, it may actually be healthier, on average, for a child to be raised by smoking parents… provided they don’t decide they like the habit enough to pick it up themselves. Now note: I am not a doctor, nor do I have any medical training whatsoever. However I can back up what I’m saying with references like this one, Multicenter case-control study of exposure to environmental tobacco smoke and lung cancer in Europe - PubMed And, of course, there are things aside from lung cancer to consider. If your parents smoke, they are, after decades of their habit, going to be more vulnerable to respiratory infections like bronchitis… and thus you’re more likely to be exposed and contract them — not because of them smoking indoors or out in the back fields of a garden, but simply because you live with them and can catch things when they are infected. If you want to play the “I am a helpless child and you are hurting me!” card against them, you could try that and at least have some truth on your side. Be careful going beyond that though… they might have read enough in the area to know you’re not really likely to be at any significant risk. Your “exposure” to serious things could well end up being LESS than that of less fortunate children whose parents don’t smoke and who live cooped up in one of those Bubble Boy shells!

Question: Can you preheat water in a shower?
Answer: I am not a plumber, but I believe that to some degree you can Or At least that you should be able to.) The tanks are designed to come on and heat the water when a thermostat senses that it has dropped below a certain temperature, say"X", and heat the tank's water back up to the top of the range you've picked as desirable, say X+15, and then shut off until the temp drops below its range again. In the course of an ordinary longish shower, if it had been mid-range at the start, it might take two minutes or so for the tank heater to come on and then it would be trying to compete with heating fresh cold water while you are simultaneously pulling out hot water. IF however, while you are in the initial stages of getting your fresh clothes etc, you had turned the hot water on at full blast for sixty or ninety seconds, you’d have triggered you heater to come on. Then you turn the water off, and spend five or so minutes getting set, and THEN adjust the faucets to your temperature and start your shower. You’ll be starting while the tanks water has been preheated to its maximum heat and the result should be a longer period of water as hot as you like. If you **REALLY** want to max this idea out, have a confederate watch and time the heater in the basement and call you on your smartphone when the heater comes on and again when it’s gone off. Do that on three occasions to get a true average and you’ll be able to use that average timing for future preheats! Heh, your confederate can also check the water heater thermostat and perhaps turn it up. HOWEVER… IF YOU SHARE THE SAME SYSTEM AS OTHERS… you need to let them know what you’re planning and get their agreement. Otherwise they might turn their shower on as usual, then hop in and find themselves with scalding water pouring on them! So yeah, SERIOUSLY, *do* check with others before making any changes!

So, if you “worked” in that home for thirty or forty years you’d have perhaps about the same. Living with them for 20 years (i.e. the other 16 hours, assuming they all stayed awake and smoked in the house while you were there) would increase your four chances in a thousand by 19% of that… i.e. about one extra chance in a thousand… giving you about 5 chances in thousand of getting lung cancer someday (perhaps a little more since you were exposed younger, or perhaps a little less because it’s unlikely they all smoked around you for more than 8 hours a day. The conclusion could also be juggled up and down a little by specifying what country you were applying the study to. Oh! There’s one extra catch that should make you even LESS worried: That extra one chance in a thousand conclusion is really only valid if you throw out the normal statistical rules calling for a 95% certainty for the EPA study. They were not able to get a number that high so they accepted a 90% conclusion as being valid. Heh… that’s not very fair of them, but hey, they’re the EPA so they made their own decision! Regular, normal, unbiased science conducted by a less powerful entity would have simply been judged unable to reach a significant conclusion of any increase at all! So, relax and enjoy your family. In the 1970s I first entered into a conflict about secondary smoke exposure and believed that people were being deliberately misled about its danger. In researching that I found my concerns validated, and that led me to question the link between smoking and lung cancer itself. HOWEVER… many, MANY hours later, after a LOT of reading (I’ve always been a bit of a research freak, particularly spurred by my studies of wartime propaganda in my college and grad school Peace Research programs.) I decided that, despite what I’d discovered about secondary smoke, the claims about the thousand-times more intense exposures to smoking itself were largely valid. Tobacco smoke clearly contains carcinogens (So does human breath and orange juice and the air you breathe almost anywhere on Earth!) but it’s not just their presence that’s important, it’s their quantity. Smoking a single cigarette is equivalent to sitting around in rooms with smokers for roughly 1,000 hours, maybe even 10,000 hours or more if the room is decently ventilated. And smokers don’t just smoke a single cigarette, they usually smoke between 100,000 and 500,000 cigarettes in the course of their lifetime… equivalent to sitting around with smokers around you for up to five BILLION or more hours (That’s equivalent to over two MILLION years of working in a smoking office environment today without a single week of vacation time!) People worrying about ordinary exposures to secondary smoke have either been deliberately misled (most often the case) or are simply neurotic (See SOTT: Recognising Anti-Smoking Types - Sott.net for more on that if you wish.) but people worrying about the million or billionfold greater exposure from smoking itself is quite reasonable. Statistically almost every study out there on the subject concludes that smokers smoking normal amounts throughout one’s whole life increases one’s chances of lung cancer by anywhere from 10x to 35x (or even more if there are co-exposures to other carcinogens.) QUALIFICATION: Fortunately for most smokers, the base rate of lung cancer (at least in the U.S.) is very low: about 1/2 of 1%.[1] So even most nonsmokers who have a working lifetime of exposure to secondary smoke in a smoking environment only get less than 1/10th of one percent extra chance at being hit with it.[2](Much less in a well-ventilated modern type smoking environment… even after that working lifetime!) And for smokers themselves, even that 10x to 35x lifetime smoking increase works out to a concrete chance of just about a 5% to 15% chance of actually getting lung cancer — a much lower figure than the headline screams lead most to generally believe. But statistically that’s a still a VERY significant increase for smokers, and one that’s VERY hard to deny or explain away by confounders or other such explanations. REASON 2: BIOCHEMISTRY. Over the last 50 to 100 years cancer has been studied to death (excuse the pun) and researchers have gotten a pretty good handle on understanding how certain chemicals can injure certain cells in ways that make it more likely that those cells will turn cancerous and start wildly reproducing to the point where people are likely to suffer and die from cancer. Non-chemical exposures exist too: radiation will do it, or even a passing, momentary splash of sunshine as you walk past a window can do it. The key thing to pay attention to here is the AMOUNT of exposure, in terms of actual amount AND in terms of concentration and duration of exposure. We’re all exposed to carcinogens pretty much all day every day in our lives at very low levels unless we constantly spend our entire existence living inside a science-fiction style clunky space-suit with an impossibly clean feed of a perfect blend of air. But the great majority of us will die from other things besides cancer. Unfortunately for smokers, cigarette smoke has enough carcinogens in it that smoking hundreds of thousands of them exposes some particularly delicate and absorptive tissue (if they inhale, which most of them do, with literally millions of direct puffs over their lives) to a good number of known chemical “Class 1” or “Class A” carcinogens. And the amounts of those carcinogens tend to be FAR greater than they’d normally get on a regular basis anywhere else in their environments. So, for cigarette smokers, the combination of amount, duration, and concentration all combine so that even if we had NO statistical reason to believe in a connection, there’d be a strong argument to classify smoking as generally carcinogenic and thus say, pretty damn confidently, “that smoking causes lung cancer.” NOW… all that being said… there IS something else to consider: MODIFICATION: Most of us smoke cigarettes that have been grown in agricultural situations that involve a LOT of “unnatural” intervention to protect the tobacco crops from pests and blight and to encourage them to grow faster and better and with the proper amounts of nicotine to satisfy government regulators’ requirements that manufacturers are able to state on a regular basis how much “tar and nicotine” is in each brand of cigarette (even though those same government regulators will turn around the following day and say such things DON’T MATTER since *All Smoking Is Deadly*! (Yes, they’re a bit schizophrenic: what else do you expect from a government, eh?) If you’re old enough to remember the 1970s/80s hippie-marijuana-discovery years when pot moved from the American Jazz Scene to mainstream college campuses and life, you may remember a book published in 1970 that the hippies loved: The Cultivator’s Handbook Of Marijuana by Bill Drake. Well, a few months ago I ran across a posting here on Quora by a fella named Bill Drake and… he was THE Bill Drake who’d authored that Handbook! LOL! I was floored! I also discovered he’d gone on to write The Cultivator’s Handbook of Natural Tobacco (!) AND was busily writing a new book whose focus would be on the chemicals in commercial cigarettes from the pesticides and herbicides and fertilizers used on standard tobacco crops. (Actually up on Amazon at Smoke No Evil: Bill Drake, Michael McFadden: 9781692097851: Amazon.com: Books) You’ll often hear about “All the chemicals Big Tobacco adds to cigarettes” but in reality most of the chemicals of concern are produced in the combustion process of the chemicals used in the growing process — not added in any real sense by Evil Big Tobacco after the fact. The problem is that even though the amounts of such chemicals are low enough that we can ignore them in our foods, they get a lot nastier when they’re burned and we inhale them with the tobacco smoke. So the basis of Bill’s new book was to be centered around those chemicals and the health implications of smoking tobacco without them. I offered to read it over and give him some free editorial advice and enjoyed it greatly. (Disclosure here: I wrote a FOREWORD to it that I’ll be putting up in one of my Spaces soon and will add a link here for any who want to read it!) I don’t think he makes a case that would totally exonerate smoking tobacco in terms of health effects, but I agree with him that it’s quite possible that a significant amount of smoking-related cancer may be caused more by the style of agriculture than by the simple burning leaves themselves! SOOoooo… OVERALL: My answer is that I believe there’s good scientific evidence, background, and statistics to link direct primary smoking of today’s standard cigarettes to a significant increase in lung cancer and to believe that such smoking is a direct cause. HOWEVER… I also believe that the enjoyment many people get from smoking makes the choice to smoke a rational one, though one that many decide not to make, either never starting or deciding to quit by ages 30 to 40 and likely avoid a substantial amount of the overall risk (lung cancer and other diseases/problems) that smoking can bring (See: UK MILLION WOMEN 97% STUDY for more on that.) AND, FINALLY: As any who’ve read my writings here before already know, I believe any risk from likely exposures to secondary tobacco smoke in reasonably ventilated situations is so far beneath ordinary concern that most current laws, regulations, and warnings about it are unnecessary, ridiculous, and often even harmful in their overall effects: they are little more than outright lies designed for social engineering rather than for public education and safety. Question: Is it correct to use "an" or "a" before a word starting with the letter F in English?
Answer: When you pronounce the letter “F” itself, either alone or as the starting sound of a word (e.g. “an effort”) you would use “an” before it. When you simply USE the letter “F” as the first letter in a word and it is not pronounced as the name of the letter, then you would use “a”. And finally, if a word starts with other letters that collectively produce the sound of the name of the letter itself (such as “effort”) then you would use “an”.
